entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
BRICS (est. as concept 2001 by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill; first formal summit 2009, Yekaterinburg, Russia; expanded to BRICS+ 2024) is the grouping of major emerging market economies — originally Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa — that was created as an investment thesis (the four largest emerging markets with the fastest-growing GDPs) and became a geopolitical bloc representing the Global South's challenge to the Western-dominated international order. BRICS members collectively represent approximately 40% of the world's population, 26% of global GDP (nominal), and 31% of global GDP (PPP).

The BRICS concept was invented by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill in a 2001 research paper ('Building Better Global Economic BRICs') as a description of the four largest emerging market economies — Brazil, Russia, India, China — with the fastest-growing GDPs. South Africa joined in 2010. The first formal BRICS summit (2009) transformed the investment concept into a diplomatic forum, and subsequent summits have established the BRICS as the primary institutional voice of the Global South challenging the dominance of Western-dominated institutions (IMF, World Bank, G7).

The New Development Bank (NDB, est. 2014, Shanghai) — the BRICS multilateral development bank — was established as an alternative to the World Bank for infrastructure financing in developing countries. The BRICS+ expansion (2024) admitted Iran, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Egypt, Ethiopia, and Argentina (though Argentina subsequently withdrew), creating a group representing 45% of the world's population. BRICS has become the primary institutional expression of multipolar world order — the geopolitical shift away from US hegemony.

 BRICS: A New Global Power Brokers 

Established in 2009 by a convergence of rising powers from the Global South, BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa) represents the most significant shift in global governance since the post-World War II era. This association is a direct response to the dominance of the Western world order, driven by institutions like the IMF and World Bank that had been deeply influenced by US interests. The founding members sought to create an alternative framework for international cooperation, one that prioritizes the interests of developing countries and challenges the economic and political hegemony of the West.






The BRICS grouping has since grown to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates, further solidifying its position as a major player in global affairs. This expansion has been accompanied by increased diplomatic engagement, economic cooperation, and strategic partnerships with countries across the world.






By doing so, BRICS seeks to redefine the rules of international relations, promote multipolarity, and create new opportunities for cooperation and collaboration among nations.






As a result, BRICS has become a focal point for discussions on globalization, development, and economic reform, with implications that extend far beyond its member countries. The significance of BRICS lies not only in its ability to provide an alternative voice to the West but also in its potential to shape the future of global governance.
